procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Judicial Magistrate (private complaint)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the ~th November, 1982 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Criminal Miscellaneous Petition No. 1936 of 1982.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants moved the High Court of Andhra Pradesh under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the criminal proceedings initiated against them. The High Court dismissed their application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by Special Leave challenging the dismissal of their application by the High Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the decision of the High Court, and quashed the complaint case.

directions: set aside the decision of the High Court
quash the complaint case filed against the appellants

issue.issue_text: Whether a prosecution for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code is maintainable on a private complaint, in the absence of a complaint by the Civil Court where the allegedly forged document was produced, in view of the bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: The appellants filed a civil suit and produced a document (a money receipt) with the plaint.
Subsequently, the respondent filed a private criminal complaint against the appellants.

The complaint alleged that the document produced in the civil suit was forged and that the appellants had committed offences under sections 467 (forgery of a valuable security) and 471 (using a forged document as genuine) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).

The appellants argued that the criminal prosecution was not maintainable because it was barred by Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), as there was no complaint from the Civil Court where the document was produced.
The High Court rejected the appellants' argument, allowing the private prosecution to continue.
law: Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the CrPC states that no court can take cognizance of any offence 'described in section 463' of the IPC, or punishable under section 471 IPC, when the offence is alleged to have been committed in respect of a document produced in a court proceeding, except on a written complaint from that court.
Section 463 of the IPC defines the offence of forgery.
Section 467 of the IPC punishes a specific, more serious category of forgery (e.g., of a valuable security).
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the offence punishable under Section 467 IPC is fundamentally an offence 'described in Section 463' IPC, as Section 463 provides the general definition of forgery.

The Court established a direct link: since Section 463 defines forgery and Section 467 punishes a particular category of that same forgery, an offence under Section 467 falls within the scope of the phrase 'offence described in section 463'.
Because the alleged forgery under Section 467 was in respect of a document produced in the Civil Court, the bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the CrPC was immediately attracted.
The Court explicitly rejected the High Court's view, stating that it 'took a wrong view of the matter'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the IPC was not maintainable on a private complaint. Since the offence under Section 467 is a type of forgery described in Section 463, and the allegedly forged document was produced in a Civil Court, the bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the CrPC applied. Therefore, a written complaint from the Civil Court was a mandatory prerequisite for the criminal court to take cognizance of the offence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a prosecution for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code is maintainable on a private complaint, in the absence of a complaint by the Civil Court where the allegedly forged document was produced, in view of the bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution is not maintainable on a private complaint because the allegedly forged document was produced in a civil court.

In view of Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, cognizance of offences under sections 467 and 471 of the IPC cannot be taken without a written complaint from the court where the document was produced.
Allowing the prosecution to continue would cause serious prejudice to the appellants as the trial would not be sustainable in law.
respondent_arguments: The bar in Section 195(1)(b)(ii) applies to offences 'described in section 463' of the IPC, but not explicitly to Section 467.
Penal provisions should be interpreted very strictly.
A strict interpretation means that Section 463 (forgery) cannot be construed to include the aggravated offence under Section 467 (forgery of a valuable security).
Therefore, it is competent for a Magistrate to take cognizance of an offence under Section 467 on a private complaint without following the procedure in Section 340 of the CrPC.

cases.case_name: S. L. Goswami v. High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur
cases.principle: An offence under Section 466 of the Indian Penal Code is an aggravated form of forgery as described in Section 463 of the IPC. When such an offence is committed in relation to a court record, it falls within the purview of Section 195(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An offence punishable under Section 467 of the Indian Penal Code, being a specific category of forgery, is considered an offence 'described in Section 463' of the same code. Consequently, when such an offence is alleged to have been committed in respect of a document produced in a court proceeding, a prosecution is not maintainable without a complaint in writing from that court as mandated by Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
obiter: Penal provisions ought to be interpreted very strictly.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An offence punishable under Section 467 of the Indian Penal Code (forgery of a valuable security) is an offence "described in" Section 463 of the IPC, which provides the general definition of forgery. Consequently, when a document allegedly forged under Section 467 is produced in a court proceeding, the bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is immediately attracted. In the absence of a written complaint from that court, a prosecution on the basis of a private complaint is not maintainable and taking cognizance of the offence would be bad in law.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory interpretation of the phrase 'any offence described in section 463' as used in Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The court determined that an aggravated form of an offence (IPC s. 467) falls within the description of the basic definition of that offence (IPC s. 463) for the purposes of the procedural bar in the CrPC.
policy_considerations: Allowing a prosecution to continue when it is not legally sustainable would cause serious prejudice to the appellants.
Appellants should not be called upon to face a trial that is not sustainable in law.
In the absence of a legally valid complaint from the court, continuing the prosecution would amount to unjustified harassment.
